AI for Mobility · Module 4 · Deep generative models · Interactive companion

Same VAE, different traffic

One network, three kinds of traffic, one model. Train the same variational autoencoder on light traffic, on heavy congestion, or on both, and the latent space it builds comes out different each time. This page shows how, and what that means for the data you collect.

Two ways to summarize a whole network in a few numbers

Suppose you can see every vehicle in a 42-intersection grid at one moment. That is 1,008 road cells, each empty or occupied. Traffic flow theory already knows one good summary of such a snapshot: count the vehicles. The macroscopic fundamental diagram (MFD) says that this one number, the load, tells you roughly how much flow the network delivers. A VAE builds its own summary, a few numbers we call knobs, and learns it from examples instead of from a formula.

The mechanism · a summary you choose vs. a summary the data chooses

Takeaway: the MFD's summary is fixed by its formula. The VAE's summary is fixed by its training data, so changing the traffic in the data changes the summary.

The network's flow–load curve · where the three kinds of traffic sit

light, load 0.05–0.15near capacity, load 0.45–0.70heavy, load 0.80–0.92

Takeaway: flow peaks at 0.131 vehicles per link per step near load 0.6. Light traffic sits on the rising side (15–42% of peak flow); heavy congestion sits on the falling side (43–81% of peak, dropping as load rises). Curve: mean of 3 runs per load, 400 measured steps each.

Why does this curve lean to the right? (optional)
signals re-picked every stepre-picked every 10 steps (this page)

Inside one link, Rule 184 treats vehicles and gaps alike: vehicles move forward one cell per step and gaps move backward one cell per step. On its own, a link therefore has a symmetric flow–density triangle. Signals break that balance when reds are long. A red holds a vehicle at the stop line for the whole red, but a link's entrance is fed by three approaches, and at least one of them has green in either phase. Going from phases re-picked every step to every 10 steps, the share of vehicles held at a red at load 0.1 rises from 26% to 34%. Over the same change, the share of gaps stuck at a link entrance at load 0.9 falls from 42% to 31%. Light traffic loses flow, heavy traffic gains it, and the peak moves right: with every-step signals the curve is close to symmetric (flow at load 0.1 is 0.95 of the flow at load 0.9, peak at 0.50); with 10-step phases that ratio is 0.61 and the peak sits at 0.58. (Both curves come from a fresh set of runs, so the green one differs slightly from the chart above.)

Measured network MFDs usually lean the other way: they peak well below half the jam density, because vehicles drive forward faster than queues travel back (measured in Yokohama by Geroliminis and Daganzo 2008; explained by Daganzo and Geroliminis 2008). Rule 184 cannot show that, since both speeds are one cell per step. This page uses 10-step phases because a red then lasts longer than the 6 steps it takes to drive a link, so real queues form at stop lines.

A small city on a donut

The data come from a cellular-automaton network simulator. It is small enough to run thousands of times, and it has queues, signals and spillback, the things that make network traffic interesting.

The mechanism · one link, one time step

Takeaway: the load is set once, at the start of a run, so each run is one controlled experiment at one load. Queues form behind red lights and spill back across intersections when links fill.

Watch the network · 60 consecutive steps after warm-up

Dark cells are vehicles; bars at each intersection show which approach has green (green/red). Lanes keep to the right of the road. Links that wrap around are drawn as half-links at the edges.

How the training data were collected

Kind of trafficTarget loadRunsSnapshots
Light0.05–0.1530012,000
Near capacity0.45–0.7030012,000
Heavy0.80–0.9230012,000
  • Each run: a random target load in the range, a fresh random seed, 150 warm-up steps, then one snapshot every 7 steps (40 per run). Cells start filled at random, so actual loads spread a little wider than the targets: light 0.04–0.18; near capacity 0.43–0.73; heavy 0.78–0.93.
  • Why 7? Signals are re-picked every 10 steps. Sampling every 10 steps would catch every snapshot at the same moment after a re-pick; 7 and 10 share no factor, so all ten moments appear.
  • Split by run: 200 runs train, 50 validate, 50 test, in every regime. No two snapshots of the same run sit on both sides of a split.
  • Every model in tabs 4–7 is trained on exactly 8,000 snapshots (200 runs' worth), so differences come from which traffic it saw, not how much. Tab 8's two extra experiments use their own sets.

Checked before collecting

The simulator started as a class notebook. Before generating any data we tested it. Vehicles were conserved exactly and every cell was always 0 or 1, but four things needed fixing: the routing let 23–25% of moves be U-turns although the code meant to forbid them; signals were re-drawn every step, so half of all green time was start-up loss; a fixed update order let eastbound and northbound traffic win every conflict, leaving southbound and westbound links about 10 percentage points fuller at half load; and the drawing showed east–west links backwards. Tab 8 shows what a VAE does when such a problem stays in the data.

Encoder, soft guess, two knobs, decoder

Every model on this page has the same shape and the same training recipe. Only the data change.

The mechanism · from 1,008 cells to two knobs and back

Takeaway: the encoder does not output a point. It outputs a soft guess, a small cloud of knob settings that could have produced this snapshot.

The loss, in one line

loss(x) = − Σcells i log p(xi | z) + KL( q(z | x) ‖ N(0, I) )
In words: pay for every cell the decoder gets wrong (the rebuild cost), then pay again for every soft guess that strays from the bell (the KL cost).
SymbolMeaning here
x, xione network snapshot; xi = 1 if cell i holds a vehicle
z = (z₁, z₂)the two knobs, a point on the latent map
q(z | x)the encoder's soft guess for snapshot x: a bell-shaped cloud with centre μ and spread σ
p(xi | z)the decoder's probability for what cell i shows, given the knobs
N(0, I)the bell: knobs centred at 0 with spread 1, the shape we want all knobs to have together. Distances on the latent map are counted in these units: 1 bell-width = a spread of 1
KLhow far the soft guess is from the bell, in nats (natural-log units of information)

The loss is the negative of the evidence lower bound (ELBO). We report it as the score of a snapshot: lower is better. A score is in nats per snapshot; dividing by 1,008 gives nats per cell.

The idea this page is about: the latent distribution of a dataset

Many soft guesses make one cloud · 40 light snapshots, light + heavy model

Takeaway: each ellipse is one snapshot's soft guess (centre ± one spread). Stack the soft guesses of every snapshot in a dataset and you get the dataset's latent distribution. The dashed rings are the bell (radius 1 and 2).

q(z) = average over snapshots x of q(z | x)
In words: the latent distribution is the pile of all soft guesses for the data you feed in. The bell is only the target the KL cost pushes toward. The pile is what the data actually make.

Two things change the pile. Change the snapshots you feed to a trained model, and you change the pile (tab 5). Change the snapshots you train on, and you change the encoder and decoder themselves, so the same snapshot lands somewhere else and the knobs mean something else (tab 4).

Going deeper (optional): why the pile never equals the bell, and what an unused knob looks like

The KL cost is paid per snapshot, so it pulls every soft guess toward the bell. The rebuild cost pulls the other way: different snapshots need different knob settings to be rebuilt well, so their soft guesses must sit apart. The trained model is a compromise. The pile covers the bell roughly, but with dense spots, thin spots and gaps wherever the data have clusters or gaps.

The KL cost also splits by knob. A knob whose KL is about 0 for every snapshot has a soft guess equal to the bell (centre 0, spread 1) no matter what the snapshot shows. It carries no information about the snapshot: an unused (inactive) knob. Counting knobs whose average KL is clearly above 0 (this page uses 0.05 nats) tells you how many numbers the model found worth paying for. Burda et al. count active units with a related test: how much a knob's centre varies across snapshots.

Sources: Kingma and Welling (2014), Auto-Encoding Variational Bayes; Bishop and Bishop (2024), Deep Learning: Foundations and Concepts, ch. 19; Hoffman and Johnson (2016), ELBO surgery (the averaged soft guess); Burda, Grosse and Salakhutdinov (2016) (counting active units).

The centres are not the whole distribution

Switch the maps to Centres only: the light-only model's dots form a thin vertical line, as if the latent distribution had no width. Switch back: the pile is about as wide as the bell. Each soft guess has its own spread, and the pile includes it.

Var(zj) = Varsnapshots( μj(x) ) + averagesnapshots( σj(x)² )
In words: how spread out the pile is along knob j = how far apart the centres sit + how wide each soft guess is.
SymbolMeaning here
zjknob j, read across the whole pile of soft guesses for a dataset
μj(x), σj(x)centre and spread of snapshot x's soft guess along knob j
Var, averagetaken over the test snapshots fed to the model

Worked example, light-only model (seed 0): along knob 1, centres 0.00 + soft guesses 0.90 = 0.90. All of that width comes from the soft guesses, so knob 1 says nothing about the snapshot. Along knob 2, centres 0.52 + soft guesses 0.09: most of the width comes from the centres, so knob 2 carries information (the load). The readouts under each map give the same split for every model.

Change the mix, keep the encoder · half-and-half model, frozen, seed 0

How far the pile sits from the bell · aggregate KL, nats, light + heavy test snapshots

Takeaway: nothing is retrained here: same encoder, same decoder, same bell. Only the mix of snapshots fed in changes, and the pile changes with it. For this model the pile is closest to the bell at 25% heavy (0.45 nats) and farthest when fed only heavy traffic (1.82 nats). Retraining is the second way the pile changes. Fed a 5%-heavy mix, the frozen half-and-half model's pile sits 0.60–0.70 nats from the bell. The model retrained on a 5%-heavy mix pulls it back to 0.25–0.29, by squeezing congestion to the rim (tab 6).

Going deeper (optional): the aggregate KL, and what the training cost really penalizes

The aggregate KL, KL( q(z) ‖ N(0, I) ), measures how far the whole pile sits from the bell. With equal numbers of each regime's test snapshots: light-only 0.09–0.11, heavy-only 0.04, half-and-half 0.39–0.58, all three 0.56–0.60, and the model trained on 5% heavy 1.73–1.79 nats (fed its own 95/5 mix instead, it sits only 0.25–0.29 nats away; 3 seeds; 8,000 Monte Carlo draws each). The specialists' piles are close to the bell; mixing regimes leaves gaps between islands.

Training never computes this number directly, yet it pays it. Training pays the KL of each soft guess, and the average of those KLs splits into two parts: the information the knobs keep about each snapshot, plus the aggregate KL. A model can therefore keep its pile close to the bell and still put different traffic in very different places. Hoffman and Johnson (2016), ELBO surgery.

Read the knobs with care

One knob always tracks the load: the same quantity the MFD uses. Beyond the load, the knobs pick up whatever pattern is left over in that training data. In light traffic it was most often the signal clock: how many steps had passed since the intersections last re-picked their phases, which decides how many vehicles are waiting at red lights. We count a knob as following the clock when phase timing explains at least 30% of its variation. That happened in 8 of the 12 two-knob models that saw light traffic (34%–52%); in the other 4, the best knob reached only 2%–14%. Which knob carried the clock also varied: in the half-and-half model it rode on the same knob that separates light from heavy. In heavy traffic the leftover pattern was where the jam sits. We found these meanings only by checking the knobs against things we had recorded (load, signal timing). The knobs are not physical parameters; they are a compression of the data, and the same data with another seed can fold them differently.

Three things a knob might mean: two hold, one does not

1. A summary. Its value can track a measured quantity: the load knob's |correlation| with the vehicle count is 0.93–0.95 in the light-only model, on runs it never saw. That holds for this model and this data, not as a law.

2. A control. Turning it changes what the decoder produces: in the heavy-only model, one knob moves about 28–30 vehicles between links.

3. Not an intervention. Turning a knob changes the model's output, not traffic. It adds no vehicles and retimes no signal. To learn what more vehicles or longer phases do, change them in the simulator, as the flow–load curve in tab 1 does.

So the direction of a knob means nothing on its own. Flip the sign of knob 1 as it leaves the encoder, and flip it back as it enters the decoder. Every rebuild and every generated network is identical, and because the bell is symmetric, the KL cost is too. Swapping the two knobs works the same way. Our 15 two-knob models show it: the load sat on knob 1 in 9 and on knob 2 in 6; a larger value meant more load in 11 and less in 4. To build meaning in, give the model the measured quantity as an input (a conditional VAE) or train one knob against it, and then test that meaning again. Locatello et al. (2019) show why unsupervised training alone cannot guarantee it.

How many knobs each diet pays for · 16-knob models, average KL per knob on test snapshots, largest first, mean of 3 seeds

Takeaway: light traffic paid for 5–6 knobs, heavy congestion for only 2–3. To see what they track (seed 0), we predicted each used knob from recorded quantities on held-out runs. Light traffic: one knob followed the load, one how vehicles sit along links (waiting at stop lines or moving), and three which links held vehicles (each explained with R² 0.74–0.86 from the 168 link densities). Heavy traffic: the load and two jam-location patterns. The extra light-traffic knobs each carry little (about 0.5–0.7 nats per snapshot), which is why the two-knob light model gave its second knob so little. Mixing usually shrank what the model kept per regime: the half-and-half model used 3, 3, 6 knobs on light traffic (light-only model: 5, 6, 6) and 1, 2, 1 on heavy (heavy-only: 3, 2, 2), seed by seed; the 6 includes four knobs at 0.05–0.07 nats, barely over the cutoff. The model trained on all three used 5–7. Grey bars: knobs below the 0.05-nat cutoff, effectively unused.

Before you trust this result

Baseline
A table of each cell's average occupancy in the same traffic (no knobs at all) scores 299.0 on light and 425.4 on heavy test snapshots. The two-knob VAEs score 296.4 (L on light) and 421.8 (H on heavy), a few nats better. (The VAE's score is an upper bound on its true cost, so the real gap is somewhat larger.) Most of a snapshot is randomness that two knobs do not predict: exactly which cells hold vehicles. What the knobs add is the load and one pattern.
Split
By run: test snapshots come from 50 runs the models never trained or validated on, at loads drawn from the same ranges.
Ugly cases
In 4 of the 12 two-knob models that saw light traffic, no knob followed the signal clock, and in the others it rode on different knobs. Maps are also flipped or swapped from seed to seed: "knob 1" in one seed can be "knob 2" in another.

Feed a model traffic it never saw

A trained model has no "I don't know". Give it a snapshot from outside its training data and the encoder still produces a soft guess, and the decoder still produces a network. Where does that guess land, and how bad is the rebuild?

Light-only model, fed all three kinds · model L, seed 0

Heavy-only model, fed all three kinds · model H, seed 0

lightnear capacityheavyarrows: dots far off the map, with their distance from the centre

The light-only model pushes congestion far outside the bell

The cloud of heavy snapshots is centred 12–16 bell-widths from the centre of the map (3 seeds; single snapshots 11–18); every one of them is beyond radius 3, where the bell puts about 1% of its draws. Their KL cost is 79–138 nats, against 1.1–1.7 for light snapshots. Here the latent position works as an alarm.

But look at the rebuild: the decoder has only ever produced light traffic, so it misses the vehicle count by 779 vehicles on average (heavy snapshots hold about 850 vehicles in their cells).

The heavy-only model keeps light traffic inside the bell

The cloud of light snapshots is centred only 1.5–1.9 bell-widths from the centre; 63%–96% of them sit inside radius 2, the same region that holds 93%–95% of the heavy test snapshots. Judged by position alone, nothing looks wrong.

The rebuild says otherwise: it misses the vehicle count by 711 vehicles (light snapshots hold about 100), and the score is 1,571.7 nats against 296.4 for the light-only model on the same snapshots.

Score of every model on every kind of test traffic · nats per snapshot (lower = better), mean of 3 seeds; in brackets, vehicles the rebuild misses

Takeaway: on its own kind of traffic every model is close to the others and to the average table. Off its diet, every model scores worse than the average table of that traffic, by 83 to 3,931 nats. The score, not the position on the map, is the reliable sign that a snapshot is unfamiliar.

Before you trust this result

Baseline
Per-cell average table of the same traffic: 299.0 (light), 666.5 (near capacity), 425.4 (heavy). Any model scoring far above these on a kind of traffic has not learned that traffic.
Split
By run; the near-capacity column was never in training for L, H, LH or the 5%-heavy model.
Ugly cases
The asymmetry held in all 3 seeds: the light model always threw heavy traffic far out (12–16), the heavy model always kept light traffic near the centre (1.5–1.9). A detector built on "distance from the centre" would have caught one failure and missed the other.

When congestion is rare, and when near-capacity traffic is missing

Field data are never balanced. Most hours are light traffic; congestion is a few peak hours, and the breakdown near capacity is shorter still. Two experiments mimic that.

Experiment A: congestion is only 5% of the data

What each model generates · 3,000 draws from the bell per seed, decoded; share by decoded load

light-like (load < 0.2)in between (0.2–0.75)heavy-like (> 0.75)

Takeaway: with 5% heavy snapshots in training, only 1.3%–1.8% of generated networks are heavy-like. With half heavy, 22%–33%.

The 5%-heavy model squeezes congestion to the rim of the bell: heavy snapshots sit 2.4–2.5 bell-widths out and pay 8.5–8.7 nats of KL, against 2.0–2.1 for light ones. The bell rarely draws from the rim, so the generator rarely makes congestion.

Rebuilding congestion also gets worse. On heavy test snapshots the 5%-heavy model scores 431.4, against 424.1 for the half-and-half model and 421.8 for the heavy-only model. That is worse than a plain per-cell average table built from the same 10 heavy runs (427.6): with 400 heavy snapshots in 8,000, the model learned congestion less well than a lookup table does.

Balanced data does not give a balanced generator either. The half-and-half model makes heavy-like networks only 22%–33% of the time, and 11%–17% of its networks fall in between: a kind of traffic it never saw.

A generator trained on raw field data tends to under-produce exactly the states engineers care about most: queues, spillback, breakdown.

Do generated near-capacity networks look like real ones? · unevenness = standard deviation of link densities across the 168 links (the heterogeneity that scatters real MFDs)

real test snapshots (average per load bin)generated by LHgenerated by LMH

Takeaway: real traffic is most uneven near capacity: some links jammed, others nearly empty (0.29–0.32 for loads 0.40–0.70). Generated networks are more even than real ones at every load, and most of all in that range (0.19–0.21, both models, all seeds); adding near-capacity data did not fix it, and neither did 16 knobs (0.20–0.21). Even rebuilding real near-capacity snapshots gives networks at 0.20, against 0.31 for the originals. Once the knobs are set, this decoder draws every cell independently, and the KL cost pays for only a few knobs, so the many ways a jam can be arranged get averaged into an even, grey network: the VAE blur from the course's VAE-to-diffusion lab. More data fixes coverage; it does not fix the model's averaging.

Physics is the referee

A generated network can look right and score well, yet still be impossible as traffic. The latent map cannot tell you. Traffic physics can: a real network only carries so much flow at a given load, and a generated network should move like a real one.

The mechanism · flow you can read off one snapshot

Takeaway: under Rule 184 a vehicle moves one cell if the cell ahead is empty, so one snapshot already fixes how many vehicles move inside the links in the next step. Queues cut that number; spreading vehicles out raises it.

Interior flow, in one line

qint = (1 / 840) · Σlinks Σi = 0…4 xi · (1 − xi+1)
In words: count the vehicles that have an empty cell right ahead of them inside their link, and divide by the 840 cell pairs (168 links × 5). That is the share of cell pairs where a move happens next step.

xi = 1 if cell i of a link holds a vehicle. Moves into the first cell and out of the stop-line cell are left out, because they depend on the signal, which a snapshot does not record. For a decoded network the cells are probabilities, and the same sum gives the expected value.

What the check finds

Walking the load knob from −2.5 to 2.5, the decoder's flow rises and then falls. The VAE did not have to learn that shape: vehicles scattered at random over the cells give an interior flow of about k(1 − k) at load k, which already rises and falls. At load 0.51 the decoder gives 83% of that random-scatter value. Real snapshots at that load give only 52%, because real vehicles queue. The decoder's peak, 0.207, is above the highest value in any of the 6,000 real test snapshots (0.188); the real near-capacity average is 0.130. The generated networks agree: every model's networks carry more flow, on average, than real ones at the same load.

The cause is the evenness from tab 6. Once the knobs are set, the decoder gives each cell its own probability and draws the cells separately. It has no way to say “these three cells are full together”, so it scatters vehicles instead of stacking them in queues, and scattered vehicles have room to move. A queue is a joint pattern across cells; with the knobs fixed, this decoder can only raise or lower each cell's chance on its own.

Why physics still matters

  • The score cannot see it. The training score rewards getting each cell's chance right, not how the cells line up. Every model's networks carry more flow, on average, than real ones at the same load, and up to 21% of the all-three model's networks beat anything real. A pile close to the bell does not help either: the light-only and heavy-only models have the roundest piles and still carry too much flow.
  • A VAE has no conservation, no capacity and no signals. It reproduces patterns in the data; it does not enforce the rules that made them.
  • Ways to bring physics in (not tested here): put flow or speed into what the model sees, use a physics check like this one as an acceptance test, add a penalty for impossible states, use a decoder that models neighbouring cells together (autoregressive or diffusion models), and keep the simulator for anything that must conserve vehicles or show the effect of an intervention.

Before you trust this result

Baseline
The real test snapshots themselves: their interior flow at each load, mean and 95% band, from 6,000 snapshots of 150 test runs.
Split
Real snapshots from test runs only; generated networks from fresh bell draws.
Ugly cases
Interior flow leaves out moves across intersections, which need the signal state. The knob walk shows decoded probabilities, so it gives the expected flow; individual generated networks scatter around it. This is one simulator: the check is the method to copy, not the numbers.

What this means for collecting VAE training data

Two more experiments first, then the lessons. Each lesson points to the result that supports it.

Experiment C: consecutive snapshots are near-copies · 16-knob model, 30 runs × 400 consecutive steps

what the validation set reportedscore on 150 brand-new runs

Takeaway: split by random snapshots, the validation set promised 392 nats; on new runs the model scored 543, 151 worse. Split by whole runs, validation said 414 and new runs gave 464 (+50). Neighbouring snapshots leak into validation. The leak also picked a worse model (543 vs 464 on the same new runs): early stopping kept training for 241–313 epochs (whole-run split: 57–63) because the near-copies in validation kept 'improving'. Bars: mean of 3 seeds; lines: seed range. Scores mix all three regimes, so they are larger than single-regime scores elsewhere on this page.

Experiment D: a simulator bug becomes "traffic" · heavy traffic, fixed update order kept vs corrected

training datagenerated by the VAE (mean of 3 seeds; line = seed range)hollow = corrected simulator

Takeaway: with the update-order bug kept, southbound and westbound links were 4.6 percentage points fuller than eastbound and northbound in the data, and 4.7 points fuller in networks the VAE generated (filled dots). With the corrected simulator (hollow dots) the same comparison gives +0.1 points in the data and +0.1 in generated networks. The model has no way to tell an artifact from traffic.

Eight lessons

  1. The latent space describes your data, not traffic in general. The same model trained on light, heavy or mixed traffic built three different maps, with different knob meanings and a different number of knobs in use (tab 4). Before reusing someone's VAE, ask what traffic it was trained on.
  2. Cover every regime the model will meet, especially the transition. Leaving out near-capacity traffic made the model worse there than a plain average table, with results that depend on the seed (tab 6, B). The breakdown regime is short in the field, so it must be collected on purpose: peak shoulders, incident days, event days.
  3. Balance, or at least know, the mix. With congestion at 5% of the data, only 1.3%–1.8% of generated networks were congested and congestion was rebuilt worse than by a lookup table (tab 6, A). Options to try (not tested here): stratify by regime, oversample the rare one, or condition the model on the regime, and say which you did in the report.
  4. Record the conditions next to every snapshot. Load, signal timing, time of day, weather, incidents. We could tell that a knob tracked the signal clock or the jam location only because those were recorded (tab 4). Without them, the knobs cannot be read or checked.
  5. Split by run, day or site, never by snapshot. Snapshots a few steps apart are near-copies. A random split hid overfitting and, through early stopping, even picked the overfit model (experiment C).
  6. Audit the data source before training. The VAE reproduced a simulator bug as if it were a traffic pattern (experiment D). The same happens with a stuck loop detector, a miscalibrated camera or a mislabelled lane: the model learns the artifact faithfully.
  7. Watch the score to spot unfamiliar traffic, and sample time with care. Every model scored worse than a plain average table on traffic outside its diet, while the latent position gave no warning in one direction (tab 5). And sampling every 7 steps against the 10-step signal re-pick was deliberate: sampling every 10 steps would have caught every snapshot at the same moment after a re-pick, so the data would show one moment of the cycle and never the rest.
  8. Let physics referee the output. Generated networks carried more flow than the real network at the same load, and up to 21% of one model's networks beat the highest real value (tab 7). Collect the quantities that let you check this, such as flow or speed next to occupancy, and test generated states against them before using them.

From the torus to real detectors

In real data……what it does to the latent space…what to collect or do
Night and off-peak hours dominate the recordMost of the bell goes to free flow; congestion is squeezed to the rim and rarely generated (experiment A)Stratify by regime or time of day; report the mix; consider a regime-conditioned VAE
Detectors see a few points, not every cellThe knobs can only encode patterns the sensors observe; a queue between detectors is invisibleMatch sensor coverage to the pattern you need (stop-bar and advance detectors for queues)
Readings are averaged over 30 s to 15 minSignal-cycle patterns (the light-traffic other knob here) are averaged away or aliasedChoose the averaging interval relative to the cycle; avoid sampling in step with it
A new corridor, city or seasonUnfamiliar traffic can land in an ordinary-looking spot on the map (tab 5)Check the score on the new site before trusting codes or samples
Faulty or stuck sensorsThe VAE learns the fault as a pattern (experiment D)Run data-quality checks first; keep fault labels; never train on raw feeds unchecked
Consecutive readings are correlatedMany rows, few independent examples; validation looks better than reality (experiment C)Count days or runs, not rows; split by day or site

Before you trust these results

Baseline
Experiment C compares two splits of the same data against the same 150 new test runs. Experiment D compares a model on data with the update-order bug against an identical model on corrected data, same loads and seeds.
Split
C: random 80/20 by snapshot vs 24/6 by run. D: 100 training runs, 20 validation runs per version.
Ugly cases
All of this is a simulator: random routing, random signals, one-lane links, a network with no boundary (it wraps around). Real networks add demand patterns, turning bays and boundaries. The lessons are about the data, and they carry over; the exact numbers do not.

Fit card and check yourself

Fit card — VAE for network traffic states

Idea in one sentence
Compress each network snapshot into a few knobs with a soft guess, and train a decoder to rebuild the snapshot from them, so you can encode, score and generate network states.
Why it works (the logic)
The rebuild cost forces the knobs to keep what varies most between snapshots (here, first the load); the KL cost keeps the knobs packed into a bell you can sample from.
Fits these tasks
Summarizing network states into a few numbers for monitoring (extraction), flagging unfamiliar or faulty data by score (classification), generating plausible test states for regimes it was trained on (generation).
Needs this data
Many snapshots from every regime you care about, split by day or run, with conditions recorded; thousands of snapshots from hundreds of independent runs or days; no labels needed. Agencies have it as detector, probe or camera data.
Breaks when
The traffic shifts outside the training mix; a regime is rare or missing; consecutive samples are counted as independent; the source has artifacts; you need sharp, uneven states (the decoder averages); generated states must obey traffic physics, which nothing in the model enforces.
Keep the classical method when
A summary is all you need: the MFD's load answers most network-performance questions, and a per-cell average table scored within a few nats of the VAE on the traffic it was fitted to. Use the VAE when you need to generate whole states or score how unusual a snapshot is, and validate it against those baselines. Keep the simulator for anything that must conserve vehicles, respect capacity, or show what an intervention does.

Where this shows up

DomainTaskDataClassical baseline
Traffic flow and operationsCompress detector snapshots of a district into a state and track it through the day; generate test states for signal-timing studiesLoop and radar detectors, probe speeds, months of 5-min recordsMFD load and flow; PCA of detector records
Agency practice (data quality)Flag stuck or failing detectors and odd days by scoreDetector feeds with maintenance logs as checksRange, persistence and flatline rules
Driving automation and ADASGenerate occupancy-grid scenes around an ego vehicle for testing perception and planningBird's-eye occupancy grids from drone or onboard sensors (highD, Waymo Open)Rule-based scenario libraries; replay of logged scenes
Road safetyEnrich rare congested or conflict states for trainingCamera near-miss events, crash-linked traffic statesExtreme-value models on surrogate safety measures

Check yourself

  1. An agency gives you a VAE trained on one year of detector snapshots from a suburban district, 80% of them overnight. You want to generate peak-hour states for a signal retiming study. What would you check first, and what would you change in the data?
    One way to answerCheck the regime mix and the score of peak-hour snapshots (tab 5, 6A). Expect congestion to be squeezed to the rim of the bell. Re-collect or re-weight by time of day, or condition the model on the period.
  2. Your VAE's first knob correlates 0.95 with network vehicle count. A colleague says "the VAE discovered the MFD." What is right and wrong in that claim?
    One way to answerRight: the load is the dominant source of variation, so the knob tracks it. Wrong: the knob did not discover the flow–load relation, and the other knob's meaning changed with the diet and the seed (tab 4). The MFD's load is a formula you can compute without a VAE.
  3. You split 100,000 one-minute snapshots from 20 days randomly into train and validation and get an excellent validation score. What do you report, and what do you rerun?
    One way to answerReport that the split was by snapshot and that neighbouring minutes are near-copies. Rerun with whole days held out (experiment C), and report the score on held-out days.
  4. A new detector's snapshots land near the centre of your VAE's latent map. Is the detector's data normal?
    One way to answerNot necessarily: the heavy-only model placed light traffic inside the bell (tab 5). Check the score against the scores of known-good data.
  5. A colleague reports that "higher z₁ means more congestion" in her traffic VAE, and wants to set z₁ to simulate a demand increase. What two things would you tell her?
    One way to answerThe direction of a knob is arbitrary: flipping its sign changes nothing the model does (tab 4), and our models put the load on either knob with either sign. And turning a knob is not an intervention: it changes the model's output, not traffic. To study a demand increase, add vehicles in a simulator, or condition the model on measured demand and test that.
  6. Your generated corridor states look realistic and score well. Before using them in a capacity study, what one physical check would you run?
    One way to answerPut the generated states on the flow–density plane next to real data, as in tab 7, and check that no state carries more flow than the corridor ever does at that density.
